I am seventy years old this year, and my back is not what it used to be. My family has five mu of flat, good land here in Quzhou County. I do not have the strength or the desire to gamble on strange crops or new tricks at my age. I will plant winter wheat and summer maize, the same double-cropping system my father taught me and the same one every sensible farmer around here uses. In early October, after running the rotary tiller to break up the wheat stubble and bury the weeds, I will sow the improved Jimai wheat variety from the county seed station. I trust it because it has never failed me in a cold winter. When the wheat comes off in early June, I will till again and immediately plant hybrid Zhengdan maize. The hybrid seed costs more, but it gives me the yield I need and the grain purchaser pays a fair price for it. I will fertilize generously because hungry crops do not forgive you: about twenty-six kilograms of nitrogen per mu for the wheat, and about twenty-two for the maize, plus compound fertilizer for phosphorus and potassium. The wheat must have four irrigations—especially at jointing and heading—so I will run the pump even though the electricity bill stings. The maize can get by with two irrigations if the summer rains cooperate. I will spray pesticides three times on the wheat and twice on the maize; I have seen whole fields lost to armyworm and rust because a farmer got lazy. I expect my wheat to yield around five hundred ten kilograms per mu and my maize around six hundred kilograms per mu. It is hard work, but it is honest work, and at seventy, honest and predictable is all I ask from the land.
